The first thing Mara’s father forgot was how to make a small pot of coffee. He still knew how to make a large one. Every morning he filled the machine to twelve cups, drank one and a half, and poured the rest into a succession of unsuitable containers. When Mara came on Sundays, there was coffee in the pickle jar, the gravy boat, and the blue vase her mother had won at a church raffle.

“You could pour it down the sink,” she said.

“I could pour your coffee down the sink,” he said, and handed her a mug.

Across the street, the city was replacing a water main. The crew arrived at seven and ate lunch at eleven fifteen, sitting along the low wall in front of the house. One Sunday Mara found her father counting them from the living room.

“Five,” he said.

“Six. There’s a man in the truck.”

“He brings his own.”

The next day she called at eleven twenty and heard unfamiliar voices in the kitchen. Her father said he couldn’t talk. He was looking for the sugar bowl.

By Thursday there was a coffee station on the front porch: mugs, sugar, a spoon on a saucer, and a handwritten sign that said PLEASE LEAVE THE SPOON. The crew left the spoon. They also left the mugs, although not always the right mugs. A red one that said WORLD’S OKAYEST DAD appeared among the good china. Mara took it inside, washed it, and put it back out.

The woman who drove the excavator was named Ruth. She had a gold front tooth and a son who sold insurance in Ohio. Mara knew these things because her father told her, and then told her again. When Mara finally met Ruth, she was surprised to find her younger than herself.

“He says you play piano,” Ruth said.

“I used to.”

“He said you’d say that.”

Mara had been trying to persuade her father to move. There was an apartment available near her, on the ground floor, with a grocery store close enough to walk to. She had taken pictures of the rooms and put them in an envelope. He kept the envelope under the short leg of the kitchen table. It was precisely the right thickness.

In October the crew reached the end of the block. They filled in the trench, laid a temporary strip of asphalt, and took away the portable toilet. On their last morning Ruth brought a cake. She had ordered it from a supermarket and asked for THANKS, FRANK, but the decorator had written THANK FRANK. Her father said it was a good idea, and somebody ought to.

Mara came on Monday instead of Sunday that week. At eleven ten, her father carried the pot out to the porch.

“They finished,” she said.

“I know.”

He set out three mugs. She watched him go back for the other two.

It was cold enough that she could see the steam. On the new asphalt someone had chalked a number and drawn a long arrow toward the curb. She thought it would be gone by the next rain, but it stayed there all winter.

No one came for coffee that Monday. At eleven forty her father took in the mugs, and she poured the coffee down the sink. Then he got out the bread and made her a sandwich. It was only when she lifted the top slice that she saw he’d cut the cheese into six little squares, arranged in two rows, the way he had when she was a child and refused to eat a slice whole. She’d forgotten about that. She put the bread back and ate the sandwich.

He moved in March. He was the one who brought it up. The basement stairs were getting to be a nuisance, he said, and someone had built them too steep. He had built them himself in 1978. Mara told him the apartment was still available. It wasn’t, but by evening she’d found another one in the same building, on the second floor, across from the laundry room. It cost eighty dollars a month more and had a better kitchen.

While they packed, he wanted to know what would happen to the spoon.

“We’ll take it,” Mara said.

“It’s not ours.”

She turned it over. The handle was stamped with the name of a hotel that had burned down before she was born.

“Where’d you get it?”

“Your mother.”

This seemed, to both of them, to settle the matter.

The first Sunday in the apartment, Mara brought bagels. Her father had made a large pot of coffee. He poured her a cup and asked whether she’d had trouble finding him.

“No,” she said, although she had gone automatically to the old house. She had pulled up in front and turned off the engine. Someone had already taken down the porch light, leaving two capped wires sticking out of the siding. The new owners were going to paint.

Across the hall a dryer stopped. A moment later it started again.

“Those people have been in there all morning,” her father said.

“Maybe their dryer broke.”

“I meant different people.”

He took a drink. Mara unwrapped the bagels. She had brought two kinds of cream cheese but no knife, and he opened a drawer and found the spoon.

For a while they ate without talking. Then a woman backed out of the laundry room, dragging a basket with a broken handle. Mara held the door for her. The woman thanked her and went three doors down, where a child opened up and immediately asked if his sheets were dry.

Mara turned back. Her father was at the counter with the coffee pot in his hand. She thought he meant to empty it and moved aside to give him the sink.

“Could you see if she takes milk?” he said.

By the time Mara reached the woman’s door, it had closed. She could hear the child inside, explaining something at great length. She stood there with her hand raised and waited for him to finish. Then she knocked.
